Experimental method
We purchased Aluminum (III) chloride hexahydrate (AlCl3.6H12O6, Purity 99.999%), titanium (III) chloride 
hexahydrate (TiCl3. 6H2O, Purity 99.999%), thiourea (SC(NH2)2, 99.9%) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH, Purity 
99.999%) from Alfa-Aser. Through the experiment, Alfa aser-made de-ionized water was used to synthesize the 
samples. First, 2 g of TiCl3.6H2O was added in one beker containing 50 ml (ml) of deionized water and starred 
for 30 min. Second, 0.5 g of NaOH was added to the second beaker with 20 ml of deionized water for 20 min. 
Then aforementioned NaOH liquid medium was conventionally added dropwise through a pipet to 50 ml of 
TiCl3. 6H2O solution and allowed to stand at room temperature for 10 min before being magnetically stirred. 
The mentioned solution was vigorously stirred for 50 min to ensure a homogenous solution. Finally, the stirred 
solvent was transferred to a 100 ml stainless steel Teflon line autoclave and kept for reaction under 150 °C for 
24 h. The temperature of the solution in the oven was gradually raised to 150 °C. Following centrifugation, the 
resultant  solution  was  repeatedly  washed  several  times  with  deionized  water  until  it  reached  a  pH  of  7.  The 
resulting mixture was transferred into a beaker and allowed to dry for 24 h at 60 °C in an oven. Furhtermore, 
Aluminum nitrate nonahydrate (Al(NO₃)₃·9H2O) and sodium sulfate (Na2SO₄) were employed as sources of 
Al3⁺/Al2⁺ and S⁶⁺, respectively with the mixture of TiCl3.6H2O in one beaker containing 50 ml (ml) of deionized 
water  and  stirred  for  30  min.  The  molar  ratio  of  dopants  to  Ti  was  maintained  at  2%.  To  facilitate  uniform 
precipitation, the pH of the solution was adjusted to ~ 9 using ammonium hydroxide. The gel was dried at 100 °C 
for 12 h, then calcined at 500 °C for 3 h in air to achieve crystallinity and dopant inclusion. The progressive 
temperature increase (5 °C/min) resulted in regulated phase development. Finally, the pure TiO2 (named = P)

Phase transition and bandgap 
modulation in TiO2 nanostructures 
for enhanced visible-light activity 
and environmental applications

Rajwali Khan1,2, Nasir Rahman2, Adhimoorthy Prasannan3, Khayriniso Ganiyeva4, 
Sabyasachi Chakrabortty5 & Sambasivam Sangaraju1

Due to its wide-ranging applications in the climate and energy fields, enhancing the visible-light 
photoactivity of TiO2 nanoparticles remains a crucial challenge in photocatalysis. Interestingly, 
this work examined the phase transition, structural, optical, and photocatalytic characteristics of 
TiO2 nanoparticles doped with Al3⁺/Al2⁺ and S⁶⁺ ions. It was observed that the anatase phase (AP) 
dominates in pure TiO2 (100%) nanoparticles, whereas the rutile phase (RP) content increases in doped 
samples, reaching 20 ± 2.1% for X1 (Al = 2%, S = 2%) and falling to 12 ± 1.2% in X4 (Al = 2%, S = 8%). 
The introduction of Al3⁺/Al2⁺ and S⁶⁺ induces oxygen vacancies (Ovs) and alters the phase stability, as 
evidenced by the reduction of transformation energy to − 0.033 eV, facilitating the AP to RP transition. 
The effective integration of dopants indicates that a redshift and intensity in the Photoluminescence 
spectrum reduced by X-series nanoparticles is due to band gap reductions (from 3.23 eV for pure 
TiO2 to 1.98 eV for X4) and distortions in the lattice generated by Al/S doping. Raman spectroscopy 
results show peak broadening and shifts due to lattice strain from dopants, which validates 
dopant incorporation via peak shifts in Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy. ESR study reveals 
paramagnetic centers in Ti3⁺-Ovs complexes, indicating defect-induced magnetic characteristics. 
When methylene blue (MB) dye is photocatalyzed under visible light exhibits increased activity and 
degradation efficiencies that are higher than pure TiO2. The pseudo-first-order kinetic results show that 
co-doping effectively improves photocatalytic activity. Rate constants of 0.017 min⁻1 for X4 are found 
to be much higher than 7.28 × 10⁻4 min⁻1 for pure TiO2 nanoparticles. Finally, anatase X-series samples 
degraded MB at a maximum rate of 96.4% in 150 min, outperforming undoped TiO2 (15%) and rutile-
TiO2 nanoparticles (65% degradation). The fundamental mechanism explains that the photocatalytic 
characteristics of TiO2 are modulated by co-doping, which is why these compounds are potential 
candidates for environmental remediation applications.

Mechanism of photodergartion of P and X series of photocatalysts under sunlight irradiation
The possible mechanism of methylene blue degradation upon exposure to X-series nanoparticles by visible light 
irradiation is illustrated in Fig. 9. Specifically, the addition of Al and S to TiO2 has resulted in a notable increase 
in the material’s photocatalytic efficiency by moving its bandgap to the visible region. This behavior (shift) is 
explained  by  the  existence  of  induced  defects  and  Al2+/Al3+  and  S6+  ions  in  the  TiO2  lattice.  Together,  these 
elements create donor energy levels that are shallow in the TiO2 forbidden region. After the X series nanoparticles 
are subjected to the visible spectrum, absorption moves the excited charge particles in the VB to these defect 
energy states and CB. These charged electrons are easily grabbed by defects and substituted ions. The separation 
of charges occurs within the photoexcited electron and the corresponding hole of the VB in TiO2 nanoparticles. 
The photo-exposed electron–hole pairs can be effectively used for a variety of photocatalytic reactions thanks to 
this charge separation. When the photoexcited electrons come into contact with oxygen (from dissolved O2), they 
can reduce to a single electron, producing extremely responsive transitory ions like the superoxide anion radical 
anion O2·. Similar to this, when water interacts with the electron holes (h+) in the VB, OH· are created (single 
electron  oxidation).  Because  of  the  exceptional  reactivity  of  these  active  radicals,  methylene  blue  molecules 
can be attacked, causing the substance to either entirely convert into water (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2) and 
or decompose into more minor parts as shown in Fig. 9114. TiO2 is used in environmental remediation, such 
as wastewater treatment, air purification, and self-cleaning surfaces, due to its mechanism. The co-doped TiO2 
nanoparticles use photocatalytic processes to reduce pollutants and promote cleaner habitats.

The co-doped TiO2 nanoparticles’ continuous photocatalytic activity over five cycles was shown by reusability 
experiments, indicating structural stability. To measure long-term environmental performance, more testing is 
recommended in actual sunlight and wastewater environments. Although future XPS and UPS studies would 
offer direct evidence of the electronic structure modifications in this work. However, the observed redshift in 
absorption edge in the UV–Vis spectra, along with PL emission quenching and changes in optical band gap 
values, indicate significant alterations in the band structure due to Al3⁺/Al2⁺ and S⁶⁺ co-doping. These optical 
characterizations provide a solid basis for interpreting the improved charge separation and visible-light response.

Conclusion
This  work  found  that  co-doping  TiO2  nanoparticles  with  Al3⁺  and  S⁶⁺  had  a  considerable  influence  on  their 
structural, optical, and photocatalytic capabilities. The introduction of these dopants was discovered to have an 
important role in modulating the anatase-to-rutile phase transition, principally by creating oxygen vacancies 
that reduce the energy barrier for this transformation. The XRD examination confirms that larger concentrations 
of  S⁶⁺  enhance  the  stability  of  the  anatase  phase,  whereas  Al3⁺  promotes  the  production  of  the  rutile  phase. 
The  study  found  that  doped  nanoparticles  had  a  more  uniform  size  distribution  and  higher  crystallinity 
than  undoped  TiO2.  Optical  testing,  including  photoluminescence  and  UV–Vis  spectroscopy,  revealed  that 
the  addition  of  Al  and  S  dopants  introduces  mid-gap  states  and  narrows  the  band  gap,  expanding  the  light 
absorption  range  into  the  visible  spectrum.  ESR  study  reveals  paramagnetic  centers  in  Ti3⁺-Ovs  complexes, 
indicating  defect-induced  magnetic  characteristics.  This  alteration  improves  TiO2  photocatalytic  activity,  as 
indicated by a substantial increase in methylene blue degradation rates when exposed to visible light. Kinetic
